messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Emily is a 41-year-old firefighter who nearly died from sepsis two years ago. She had been fighting a wildfire when a lung infection spiraled into respiratory failure. During her three-week hospitalization, she remembers the antiseptic burn of the ICU, the sight of a central line threaded into her neck, and the sensation of her body going still as doctors worked around her. She cannot put that night into words—the terror returns as a physical collapse, her limbs frozen, the oxygen mask pressing against her face. Even now, recalling the event floods her with the same helpless dread.

In the months after her discharge, hospital smells became inescapable triggers. The faint bleach of a restroom or the alcohol wipe a paramedic uses sends her heart pounding and her body into full alert. She began scanning her surroundings constantly—checking for the gleam of a needle, listening for the hiss of an IV pump. This hypervigilance made her hypersensitive to any medical cue, so that an ambulance siren blocks away would make her chest tighten before she even knew why. Her body stays tense, ready to react, and she feels her pulse spike whenever a colleague coughs or the station’s first-aid kit is opened.

To manage the memories, Emily tries to redirect her thoughts. When the ICU scene intrudes—often during quiet moments or when she feels strong emotion—she forces herself to focus on something else, like a mental list of chores or her daughter’s piano recital. But this redirection barely contains the terror; soon after, the fragmented images return, heavier each time. She has also come to avoid emotional stress altogether. At the firehouse, she steps away from tense scene debriefings and avoids talking about the wildfire. She refused her annual physical last year, reasoning that she felt fine, and she now drives an extra ten minutes to avoid passing the hospital where she was treated.

These maladaptive strategies feed back into her threat system. By steering clear of medical settings and emotional conversations, she never learns that those places are safe; instead, her hypervigilance endures, and her body remains on a hair-trigger. Redirecting works only momentarily—the memories press back with greater force, and the terror on recall keeps her alert system chronically activated. She is caught in a loop: a hospital smell triggers scanning, which makes her avoid the source, which leaves her unprocessed memories even more intrusive, which in turn fuels her constant watchfulness.

The toll has become concrete. At work, she once prided herself on staying calm under pressure; now she avoids scenes that involve medical aid or emotional victims, and her crew captain has noticed her pulling back during calls. Last month, a routine station inspection—which included a brief tour of the on-site medical office—triggered a panic attack so severe that she could not breathe. She sat in the locker room afterward, ashamed and terrified, and finally told her husband that something was wrong. She is now seeking therapy in part because she cannot keep avoiding her own occupation. What frightens her most is the thought of being examined by a doctor again—but she is equally afraid that if she does not find a way through this, she will lose the career that has defined her for fifteen years.
